'''David R. Soll''' (born April 29, 1942) is a professor of Biology at the University of Iowa. He is best known for the motion analysis of living cells, the discovery of ''[[Candida albicans]]'' [[phenotypic switching]] and [[monoclonal antibody]] technology.   

Soll directed the [[Developmental Studies Hybridoma Bank]] from 1995 to 2021, and the WM Keck Dynamic Image Analysis Facility from 1985 to 2021. 

A fellow of both the American Academy of Microbiology and the American Association for the Advancement of Science since 2006, he has published more than four hundred articles in various fields of biomedicine.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David_Soll/publications |title=Profile: David R Soll |website=[[ResearchGate]]}}</ref> A recipient of more than seventy-eight grants and contracts,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://reporter.nih.gov/|title = RePORT ⟩ RePORTER}}</ref> he has also founded four companies, and is active on several editorial boards for major scientific publications.<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://www.oxfordjournals.org/our_journals/mmy/editorial_board.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150211194354/http://www.oxfordjournals.org/our_journals/mmy/editorial_board.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=2015-02-11 |title = Editorial Board}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/19493592/homepage/EditorialBoard.html |title = Cytoskeleton|doi = 10.1002/(ISSN)1949-3592}}</ref>

==Background==
Soll was born in South [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]], and graduated from [[Central High School (Philadelphia)|Central High School]] for Boys in 1959 with a bachelor of arts degree. He was inducted into the Central High School Hall of Fame in 2018.  

A student at the [[University of Wisconsin]] from 1960 to 1969, he earned his bachelor of science, master of science and doctor of philosophy degrees there. He then served as a post-doctoral fellow at [[Brandeis University]], where he taught Introductory Biology.

In 1972, he joined the Department of Biology at the [[University of Iowa]] as an assistant professor, was promoted to associate professor in 1976 and to full professor in 1982. In 1989, he was awarded the Roy J. and Lucille Carver/Emil Witschi Professorship of the Biological Sciences; he also became a full professor of Dentistry that same year. 

In 2005 and 2006, respectively, he was elected as a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (AAAS) and the [[American Academy of Microbiology]]. In 2009, he was awarded the Lucille K. George Medal from the [[International Society for Human and Animal Mycology]], and in 2013, he was awarded the Rhoda Benham Medal from the Medical Mycological Society of the Americas.
 
==Family==
Soll was married for thirty years to Michele Morice (1980-2010), and is currently married to Dr. Melinda A. Weinstein. He has three children, [[Jacob Soll]], Samantha Soll and Benjamin Soll.

==Career==
From 1965 to 1970, Soll worked on the germination of ''Blastoclandiella emersonii'' under the mentorship of David Sonneborn and discovered that complex differentiations can be preprogrammed and occur without RNA or [[Protein biosynthesis|protein synthesis]].<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 5277101
| pmc = 388960
| year = 1971
| last1 = Soll
| first1 = D. R.
| title = Zoospore germination in Blastocladiella emersonii: Cell differentiation without protein synthesis?
| journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
| volume = 68
| issue = 2
| pages = 459–63
| last2 = Sonneborn
| first2 = D. R.
| doi=10.1073/pnas.68.2.459
| bibcode = 1971PNAS...68..459S
| doi-access = free
}}</ref>  

From 1972 to 1978, he and his colleagues worked on the "accumulation and erasure of morphogenetics information" in ''[[Dictyostelium discoideum]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 1239391
| year = 1975
| last1 = Soll
| first1 = D. R.
| title = Morphogenesis in the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum. 1. The accumulation and erasure of "morphogenetic information"
| journal = Developmental Biology
| volume = 47
| issue = 2
| pages = 292–302
| last2 = Waddell
| first2 = D. R.
| doi=10.1016/0012-1606(75)90283-3
}}</ref> In 1979, he formulated the first model and conditional methods to analyze timer pathways in developing systems.<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 419408
| year = 1979
| last1 = Soll
| first1 = D. R.
| title = Timers in developing systems
| journal = Science
| volume = 203
| issue = 4383
| pages = 841–9
| doi=10.1126/science.419408
| bibcode = 1979Sci...203..841S
}}</ref> From 1977 to 1984, he developed pH-regulated dimorphism and applied it to study the regulation of the bud-hypha transition in ''[[Candida albicans]].''<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 6339518
| pmc = 2112305
| year = 1983
| last1 = Soll
| first1 = D. R.
| title = Filament ring formation in the dimorphic yeast Candida albicans

| volume = 96
| issue = 2
| pages = 486–93
| last2 = Mitchell
| first2 = L. H.
| doi=10.1083/jcb.96.2.486
}}</ref> 

Between 1985 and 1987, Soll and his colleagues discovered the first high frequency [[Phenotypic switching|switching system]] in the pathogenic yeast ''[[Candida albicans]].'' In addition to this phenotypic, morphological switching system, he and his co-workers also discovered the epigenetic, phenotypic [[white-to-opaque switching]] system.<ref>{{cite journal|title="White-opaque transition": a second high-frequency switching system in Candida albicans.|date=1987| pmc=211752 | pmid=3539914|volume=169|issue=1|journal=J Bacteriol|pages=189–97|vauthors=Slutsky B, Staebell M, Anderson J, Risen L, Pfaller M, Soll DR|doi=10.1128/jb.169.1.189-197.1987}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 3901258
| year = 1985
| last1 = Slutsky
| first1 = B
| title = High-frequency switching of colony morphology in Candida albicans
| journal = Science
| volume = 230
| issue = 4726
| pages = 666–9
| last2 = Buffo
| first2 = J
| last3 = Soll
| first3 = D. R.
| doi=10.1126/science.3901258
| bibcode = 1985Sci...230..666S
}}</ref>  

In 1989, Soll and Dr. E. Voss finished and licensed the Dynamic Motion Analyses System (DMS), to Motion Analyses Corporation of Santa Rosa, CA. In 1997, Soll and Voss obtained the patent for DIAS,<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5655028 | title=Dynamic image analysis system}}</ref> the next generation of DMS. In 1992, Soll founded the company Solltech, Inc., a computer software and hardware development company to develop and distribute DIAS.<ref>{{Cite book
| pmid = 8522423
| year = 1995
| last1 = Soll
| first1 = D. R.
| chapter = The Use of Computers in Understanding How Animal Cells Crawl
| title = International Review of Cytology
| volume = 163
| pages = 43–104
| doi = 10.1016/S0074-7696(08)62209-3
| isbn = 9780123645678
}}</ref>  

From 1987 to 1995, Soll and his co-workers developed the first DNA fingerprinting probes for studying the population structure of infectious fungi, and in 1995 received a patent for the software DENDRON, which analyzed DNA fingerprints.<ref>{{Cite journal
| pmid = 10756003
| pmc = 100156

| first1 = D. R.

| journal = Clinical Microbiology Reviews
| volume = 13
| issue = 2
| pages = 332–70
| doi=10.1128/cmr.13.2.332-370.2000
}}</ref>  

In 1995, Soll formed the company Caviforce Technologies to develop a method of using ultrasound for [[Germination|seed germination]]. From 1995 to 2004, he and his colleagues developed the first 3D Dynamic Image Analysis System (3D-DIAS) for cells and [[Embryo|embryos]], describing how embryos form and [[Amoeboid movement|amoeboid cells crawl]].<ref>{{cite journal

Ultrasound Solutions Inc., was then formed in 1999 to develop the technology to use ultrasound in waste management.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.news-releases.uiowa.edu/2000/may/0526swineodor.html |title=UI biologist receives grant to study acoustic management of swine odor - University News Service - the University of Iowa |access-date=2015-02-11 |archive-date=2015-02-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150211201420/http://www.news-releases.uiowa.edu/2000/may/0526swineodor.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url = https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/05/000531072419.html| url-status = dead| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150211201443/http://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2000/05/000531072419.html| archive-date = 2015-02-11| title = Help Page -- ScienceDaily}}</ref>  

In 2003, Soll founded the company Solltechnologies Inc., to sell DIAS and Dendron software. Since 2005, he and his colleagues discovered that ''[[Candida albicans]]'' forms a "pathogenic" biofilm and a "sexual" biofilm, depending on the configuration of the [[Mating-type locus|mating type locus]] and identified the alternative pathways regulating each biofilm.<ref>{{Cite journal

| doi = 10.1038/sj.emboj.7601099

From 2011 to present, Soll and his colleagues also developed a 4D model for reconstructing and motion analyzing cancer cells and [[Carcinogenesis|tumorigenesis]].

==Current Work==
Soll continues to publish on 1) the role of mating and switching in the pathogenesis of [[Candida albicans]], 2) cell motility and the [[cytoskeleton]], 3) advanced monoclonal [[antibody]] technology and 4) methods for suppressing tumorigenesis in cancer patients using monoclonal antibodies. In 2019, he began{{when|date=June 2022}} adapting the software programs DIAS and DENDRON to study digitized fine art paintings. <ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.digitalhumanities.org/dhq/vol/13/3/000423/000423.html |journal=Digital Humanities Quarterly |title=Dendrography and Art History: a computer-assisted analysis of Cézanne's Bathers |first1=Melinda |last1=Weinstein |first2=Edward |last2=Voss |first3=David |last3=Soll |date=2019 |volume=13 |issue=3}}</ref>
